LONDON, England (CNN) -- It is time for this debate to be settled once and for all: football or soccer?

What do you think the round-ball game should be called?

While it may seem like a simple discussion, the question of whether the beautiful game should be called “football” or “soccer” remains one of the sport’s most fundamental debates.

At first glance, the answer appears straightforward. The world governing body, FIFA, includes the word “football” in its name. End of story? Not quite.

The term “soccer” was coined in England in the 1880s as slang for “association.” According to the Oxford University Association Football Club’s website, former England captain Charles Wreford-Brown is commonly credited with originating the term.

“Soccer” would have been used to distinguish association football from university sports such as rugby football, known as “rugger.” Therefore, contrary to popular belief, “soccer” is a British term, not an American one.

The word is more commonly used in countries that play other forms of football. Americans, for example, also play gridiron football, while Australians play “Aussie Rules” football — an entirely different sport.

In the United States, soccer was initially referred to as football. In 1913, the United States of America Football Association was formed. In later years, it became the United States Soccer Football Association, and today it is known as the United States Soccer Federation.

Meanwhile, Australia now has the Football Federation of Australia, though it is hard to imagine the national side’s “Socceroos” nickname changing anytime soon. “Footyroos” does not quite have the same ring to it.

Now, if you are sitting in Britain reading this and wondering why there should be any debate at all about the name of football, consider this: one of Britain’s most popular shows is called “Soccer Saturday.” So perhaps the issue is not as clear-cut as it may seem.

Even the sport’s governing body appears open to both terms. At next year’s FIFA World Cup in South Africa, the area where fans will gather during the tournament is to be called “Soccer City.”

Maybe the word “football” simply does not always work.

We would like you to tell us whether the game should be called football or soccer — and why. Let us know in the SoundOff box below. You can also vote in the quick poll on the Football Fanzone homepage. Or, if you really want to make your case, why not post a video or photos on the Football Fanzone page at iReport.com?

LONDON, England (CNN) — The argument may finally need a definitive answer: should the sport played with a round ball be called football or soccer?

At first glance, the issue appears straightforward. FIFA, the sport’s global governing organization, includes the word “football” in its name. That might seem to settle the matter — but it does not.

Although many people assume otherwise, “soccer” did not originate in the United States. The word began in England in the 1880s as a slang version of “association,” referring to association football. According to the Oxford University Association Football Club’s website, former England captain Charles Wreford-Brown is often credited with creating the term.

The nickname helped distinguish association football from rugby football, which was known as “rugger” in university sporting circles. So, despite common belief, “soccer” is actually a British expression.

Today, the word soccer tends to be used more often in nations where other games are also called football. In the United States, for example, gridiron football is widely played. In Australia, “Aussie Rules” football refers to an entirely separate sport.

In fact, the game was first known as football in the United States. The United States of America Football Association was established in 1913. Over time, its name changed to the United States Soccer Football Association, and it is now called the United States Soccer Federation.

Australia, meanwhile, has the Football Federation of Australia, though it is difficult to imagine the national team abandoning its famous “Socceroos” nickname anytime soon. “Footyroos” simply does not have the same ring.

Readers in Britain may wonder why the name of football is even up for discussion. But it is worth remembering that one of the country’s best-known television programs is called “Soccer Saturday,” which suggests the issue is not as simple as it may seem.

Even the sport’s authorities appear willing to use both terms. At the following year’s FIFA World Cup in South Africa, the main fan gathering area during the tournament was set to be called “Soccer City.”

Perhaps “football” does not always fit every context. The debate over whether the sport should be called “football” or “soccer” remains one of the most familiar and unresolved discussions among fans around the world. For many supporters, especially in countries where the sport is dominant, “football” feels like the natural and traditional name because the game is primarily played with the feet. However, in other parts of the world, the word “football” already refers to different sports, which has made “soccer” a practical alternative.

Importantly, the term “soccer” did not originate in the United States, as is sometimes assumed. It actually began in England in the 1880s as slang for “association football.” At the time, different forms of football were being organized and distinguished from one another, including rugby football. “Association football” was shortened informally, and “soccer” developed from that abbreviation. This means that the word has English roots and was once part of British sporting language.

Today, “soccer” is most commonly used in countries where another sport is already known as football. In the United States, for example, “football” usually refers to American football. In Australia, the term can refer to Australian rules football or rugby league, depending on the region. Because of this, “soccer” helps avoid confusion and clearly identifies the global game governed by association football rules.

The history of the sport’s name in the United States also reflects this complexity. The country’s national governing body originally used “football” in its name, showing that the term was not completely foreign to American usage. Over time, however, the federation adopted “soccer” in its official name, now known as the United States Soccer Federation. This change reflected the broader American sporting landscape, where “football” had already become strongly associated with the gridiron game.

Even in Britain, the distinction is not as absolute as it may seem. Although “football” is by far the more common term there today, “soccer” still appears in certain contexts, such as media references, historical discussions, and phrases used to distinguish the sport from other codes of football. This continued use demonstrates that the contrast between “football” and “soccer” is not entirely clear-cut. Rather than being a simple divide between British and American terminology, the history of the words shows a more complicated and shared linguistic background.

The debate over whether the world’s most popular sport should be called “football” or “soccer” is often treated as a simple cultural disagreement: most of the world says “football,” while Americans say “soccer.” But the history of the two words is more complicated than that. Both terms have legitimate roots, and their usage has changed over time depending on region, sporting culture, and the need to distinguish between different kinds of football.

The word “football” is the older and more universal term. It naturally refers to a game played primarily with the feet, and in most countries it is the standard name for association football. Across Europe, South America, Africa, and much of Asia, “football” or a direct translation of it is the common everyday term. For many fans, this makes “football” feel like the correct and authentic name of the sport.

However, the term “soccer” did not originate in the United States, as many people assume. It began in Britain in the nineteenth century. At the time, several different football codes were developing, including rugby football and association football. To distinguish between them, British speakers shortened “association football” to “assoc,” and from that came the slang word “soccer.” This pattern of adding “-er” to shortened words was common in British university slang. In the same way, rugby football was sometimes called “rugger.”

For many years, “soccer” was used comfortably in Britain alongside “football.” It was not originally seen as an Americanism or as an incorrect term. In fact, British newspapers, schools, and sports institutions used the word at various points, especially when clarity was needed. Over time, however, “football” became the dominant everyday term in Britain, particularly as association football became the country’s leading football code. As a result, “soccer” gradually came to sound less natural to many British ears, even though it had British origins.

In the United States, the situation developed differently. American football became the dominant sport known simply as “football,” so another name was needed for association football. “Soccer” was the obvious choice because it already existed in English and clearly separated the sport from American football. For this reason, “soccer” became the standard term in American usage. The same pattern occurred in other countries where another football code became culturally dominant.

Australia provides a useful example. There, “football” can refer to different sports depending on the region, including Australian rules football, rugby league, rugby union, or association football. Because of this, “soccer” has often been used to avoid confusion. In recent decades, Australian sporting bodies have increasingly promoted the word “football” for association football, as seen in names such as Football Australia and the A-League’s official branding. Still, many Australians continue to use “soccer” in everyday speech, especially when distinguishing it from other football codes.

Official sporting bodies also show that the naming issue is not as simple as one term being right and the other wrong. The sport’s global governing body, FIFA, uses the full name “Fédération Internationale de Football Association,” reflecting the international preference for “football.” National organizations, however, have varied in their naming practices. Some historically used “soccer” in their titles, while others later changed to “football” to align with global usage and to emphasize the sport’s international identity.

The argument over the name often carries cultural meaning beyond the word itself. For some football fans, especially outside North America, “soccer” can sound foreign, commercial, or disconnected from the sport’s traditions. For many Americans, on the other hand, “soccer” is simply the normal and practical word for the game. Neither side is using a term without historical basis. The difference comes from local sporting landscapes and the way language adapts to avoid ambiguity.

Ultimately, both “football” and “soccer” are historically valid names for the sport. “Football” is the dominant global term and reflects the game’s central identity in most countries. “Soccer,” however, is not an American invention or a mistaken label. It originated in Britain as a nickname for association football and survived in places where “football” already referred to another sport. The naming debate therefore reveals less about correctness and more about history, culture, and the changing meanings of words across the English-speaking world.

# Football or Soccer? The Great Naming Debate Still Kicks On

It is the world’s most popular sport, played from packed stadiums in Madrid and Manchester to dusty pitches in Lagos, Buenos Aires and Mumbai. But one question continues to divide fans — sometimes as fiercely as any derby:

**Should it be called football or soccer?**

For many supporters around the globe, the answer is obvious. The game is played primarily with the feet, so it is football. In the United Kingdom, Europe, South America, Africa and much of Asia, “football” is the default term, tied to generations of club loyalty, World Cup drama and local identity.

But in the United States, Canada, Australia and a handful of other countries, “soccer” remains common — largely because “football” already refers to other popular codes, such as American football, Canadian football or Australian rules football.

## Where did “soccer” come from?

Despite what some fans may think, the word “soccer” is not an American invention.

The term traces back to England in the late 19th century, when different forms of football were being organized under formal rules. Two major versions emerged: **rugby football** and **association football**.

“Association football” referred to the game governed by the Football Association, founded in England in 1863. British university slang often shortened words and added “-er” to the end. Rugby football became “rugger,” and association football became “assoccer,” later shortened to **“soccer.”**

So while “football” may be the older and more globally dominant term, “soccer” has deep British roots.

## Why does the debate matter?

For some fans, the name is about tradition. Calling it football reflects the sport’s history and its global culture. It is the language of the World Cup, the Champions League and countless local rivalries.

For others, “soccer” is simply practical. In countries where another sport already owns the word “football,” using “soccer” avoids confusion.

Still, language in sports is never just language. It carries identity, geography and pride. A single word can signal where a fan is from — and sometimes how they see the game itself.

## Have your say

So, what should the sport be called?

Is **“football”** the only proper name for the beautiful game?  
Is **“soccer”** a perfectly valid term with a legitimate history?  
Or does it depend on where you are watching, playing or cheering?

Join the debate in the comments and tell us: **football or soccer — which side are you on?**

**Why Do Some Countries Call Football “Soccer”? Let’s Settle This Like Sports Fans**

Few words in sport can start an argument faster than **“soccer.”**

In much of the world, the game is simply **football** — and that makes sense. You play it mostly with your feet. But in countries like the United States, Canada, Australia, and historically parts of Ireland and South Africa, the word **soccer** has been widely used to distinguish association football from other popular football codes, such as American football, Canadian football, Australian rules football, rugby league, or rugby union.

So where did “soccer” come from?

Surprisingly to some, the word is not an American invention. It comes from Britain.

In the 19th century, different forms of football were being organized and given formal rules. **Association football** was the version governed by the Football Association, while **rugby football** followed a different path. British university slang often shortened words and added “-er” to them. So “association” became “assoc,” then “soccer.”

One name often linked to the popularization of the term is **Charles Wreford-Brown**, an English sportsman and football administrator. The story goes that when asked whether he wanted to play “rugger” — rugby football — he replied that he preferred “soccer.” Whether the tale is perfectly precise or polished by time, Wreford-Brown remains part of the word’s folklore.

The term then traveled. In places where another “football” already dominated, “soccer” was useful. Australia is a great example. With Australian rules football and rugby codes deeply established, “soccer” helped identify the round-ball game clearly. That’s also why Australia’s national men’s team is famously known as the **Socceroos** — a nickname that blends “soccer” with kangaroos and has become part of the country’s sporting identity.

Still, language in sport is emotional. To many fans, “football” feels traditional, global, and correct. To others, “soccer” is practical, historically valid, and culturally specific.

Maybe the real answer is this: the name depends on where you are, what game your community grew up calling “football,” and how much you enjoy arguing in comment sections.

So what do you think: should the sport be called **football** everywhere, is **soccer** perfectly acceptable, or does it not matter as long as the match is good?

# Football or soccer? What you call the world’s game depends on where you are

Around much of the world, the answer is simple: It’s football.

But in the United States, Canada, Australia and a few other places, the word “soccer” is still commonly used to describe the sport played with a round ball, two goals and very little use of the hands. The difference can spark friendly arguments, national pride — and plenty of confusion during major tournaments.

So where did the two names come from?

The word “football” has been used for centuries to describe various games played on foot, many of them involving kicking. In the 19th century, as schools and clubs in Britain began formalizing rules, different versions of the game emerged. One became rugby football. Another became association football — the game now governed internationally by FIFA.

“Soccer” is often assumed to be an American invention, but its roots are British. The term developed as slang from “association,” shortened to “assoc” and eventually “soccer.” For decades, both “football” and “soccer” were used in Britain, though “football” became the dominant term there and across most of the globe.

In the United States, the word “football” was already attached to the gridiron game that evolved from rugby and became one of the country’s most popular sports. To avoid confusion, “soccer” stuck. Similar naming patterns can be found in countries where another code of football — such as Australian rules football, rugby league or Gaelic football — has a strong following.

Today, usage often reflects local sports culture. In England, Brazil, Spain, Nigeria and much of the world, “football” means the global game. In the U.S., “soccer” remains widely understood, although “football” is increasingly used by some fans, clubs and broadcasters who want to align with international terminology.

The debate is about more than vocabulary. For some, “football” signals tradition and global identity. For others, “soccer” is practical — a way to distinguish one sport from another in places where “football” already means something else.

Either way, the game itself is the same: 22 players, one ball and a worldwide audience that can turn a single match into a shared global moment.

Is it football, soccer — or something else where you live? Does the name matter, or is the debate just part of the fun?

## Football or Soccer? The Global Name Game Behind the Beautiful Game

Few sports unite the world like the beautiful game — and few spark such a familiar argument over what to call it. Is it **football**, the name used across much of the globe, or **soccer**, the word still common in countries where other codes of football dominate?

In **Britain**, the answer seems obvious today: it is football. The word “soccer,” though often treated as an American invention, actually began in England as a nickname for “association football,” used to distinguish it from rugby football. Over time, however, British fans largely dropped the term, and “football” became the standard.

In the **United States**, “soccer” remains the everyday name, largely because “football” already belongs to the NFL and the gridiron game. The same is true in **Australia**, where Australian rules football and rugby league have long competed for the word “football.” There, “soccer” has often been used to avoid confusion, though the sport’s national governing body now brands itself as Football Australia.

Globally, the sport’s official voice is **FIFA** — the Fédération Internationale de Football Association — and its name leaves little doubt about the international preference. Yet FIFA’s own tournaments are watched by fans who use both words, depending on where they live.

The debate was on full display during the **2010 World Cup in South Africa**, the first held on the African continent. Broadcasters and fans from Britain spoke of football fever, while many American outlets covered the rise of soccer’s popularity. In South Africa itself, “football” was widely used, though the country’s diverse sporting culture also includes rugby and cricket.

So which name is right? In truth, both are. “Football” reflects the sport’s global identity, while “soccer” carries its own history and practical use in countries with rival football codes. Whatever it is called, the game remains the same: 22 players, one ball, and a worldwide passion that needs no translation.
